pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–12 years

- **Topic:** Energy Loss Between Trophic Levels

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 'Interactions and interdependencies'):** builds on food webs — pupils explain why food chains are short and why producers vastly outnumber top consumers, in terms of energy transfer.

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-LS2-3):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS2-1, MS-ESS2-4, MS-LS1-6, MS-LS2-3] — energy loss at each transfer is the quantitative heart of that model.

- **Operational details:** The core idea: only a small fraction (~10% as a teaching rule of thumb) of the energy at one trophic level is passed on to the next; the rest is 'lost' as heat from respiration, in movement, and in undigested/uneaten material. Consequences the pupil must derive: (a) each level up has far less available energy, so supports far less biomass — hence the pyramid SHAPE; (b) food chains are short (rarely more than 4–5 links) because too little energy remains to support higher levels; (c) it is more energy-efficient to eat lower down the chain. Introduce the biomass/energy pyramid as the canonical representation and connect the wide-base/narrow-top shape directly to the ~10% rule.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B–C (relational moving to quantitative). Pupils apply the ~10% rule to explain pyramid shape and chain length, and can do a simple proportional calculation (10,000 → 1,000 → 100 → 10). Success = explains WHY the pyramid narrows and WHY chains are short in energy terms, not just states the rule.
bestPractices: Anchor the abstract rule in a concrete worked chain (10,000 → 1,000 → 100 → 10 kJ) so pupils see the proportion compound and the top level's tiny share.
Name WHERE the energy goes — heat from respiration, movement, waste, uneaten parts — so 'lost' means transferred out of the chain, not destroyed (respect conservation of energy).
Derive the pyramid shape and short chain length FROM the rule rather than presenting them as separate facts — the shape is the consequence.
Link to a real-world implication (eating lower on the chain feeds more people) to make the efficiency argument concrete.
Distinguish energy flow (one-way, lost at each step) from matter cycling (recycled) — pupils conflate the two constantly.
keyRepresentations: Energy/biomass pyramid — wide producer base, narrow top — the canonical shape
Worked energy chain with numbers dropping by ~90% each step (10,000 → 1,000 → 100 → 10)
Loss-arrow diagram: at each transfer, branches peel off for heat/respiration, movement, waste, uneaten
Side-by-side of a short chain (viable) vs an over-long chain (energy exhausted) to show why chains end
commonMisconceptions: Thinking energy is 'used up' or destroyed rather than transferred out of the chain as heat/waste (violating conservation of energy).
Believing energy is passed on efficiently, so it's puzzling why chains are short or pyramids narrow.
Confusing energy flow (one-way, lost each step) with matter/nutrient cycling (recycled) — assuming energy also cycles.
Assuming top predators have the most energy because they are biggest/strongest, rather than the least available energy.

learn.summary: For 11–12 year-olds: energy loss between trophic levels. The core idea is that only roughly 10% (a teaching rule of thumb) of the energy at one level passes to the next; the rest is transferred OUT of the chain — as heat from respiration, energy used in movement, and energy in undigested waste and uneaten parts — not destroyed. Pupils should derive, not merely state, that this is WHY energy pyramids are always wide at the base and narrow at the top (and biomass pyramids usually are), WHY food chains rarely exceed four or five links, and why eating lower on a chain feeds more people. Note that pyramids of numbers can be inverted (e.g. one oak tree supporting many caterpillars), because they count individuals rather than energy or mass. Anchor everything in the compounding worked chain 10,000 → 1,000 → 100 → 10 kJ.

activities.title: Watch the energy leak up the pyramid
feedback: If a learner says the missing 90% is destroyed or 'used up', redirect: energy is never destroyed, only transferred — name the exits (heat from respiration, movement, undigested waste) so all 90% is accounted for.

If a learner cannot say why the chain ends, point them back to the running total: in this model, once it has shrunk to ~10 kJ (a thousandth of the starting energy) there is too little left to support another level.
If a learner expects top predators to be most numerous, rebuild from the rule: each level up has about a tenth of the energy, so it can support far less biomass regardless of body size.
activities.rationale: Seeing the proportion compound and the top level's tiny share, then hitting the 'no energy left' wall, is intended to let pupils derive pyramid shape and chain length rather than being told them. An efficiency control makes clear the shape follows from transfer efficiency. Animated loss tokens, a running energy counter and a disabled/greyed 'add a level' control when energy is exhausted are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete; they are not required.
sourceClaims: Roughly 10% of energy is passed to the next trophic level; the rest is lost as heat from respiration, in movement, and in waste/undigested and uneaten material — this explains the pyramid shape and short chains.
NGSS MS-LS2-3: [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS2-1, MS-ESS2-4, MS-LS1-6, MS-LS2-3].
learnerActions: Start with a fixed pot of energy (e.g. 10,000 kJ) at the producer level at the wide base.

Move up one level and track what reaches it: roughly 10% passes on while about 90% peels off along labelled streams — heat from respiration, energy burned in movement, energy locked in waste and uneaten parts.
Follow the running total up the levels: 10,000 → 1,000 → 100 → 10 kJ, saying the proportion lost each step aloud.
Try to add a fifth or sixth level and notice there is essentially no energy left to support it; state in your own words why food chains are short.
Change the transfer efficiency between 5%, 10% and 20% and describe how the pyramid steepens or flattens and how many levels become possible.
activities.intendedInsight: Because only about a tenth of the energy survives each transfer, far less energy — and therefore usually far less living mass — is available at each higher level, which gives the energy pyramid its wide-base/narrow-top shape, makes most biomass pyramids the same shape, and limits chain length. 'Lost' means transferred out as heat/movement/waste, obeying conservation of energy.

activities.title: Lift-the-flap pyramid for pre-teaching and reference
feedback: If a learner only recites '10% passes on', ask them to also name where the other 90% goes (heat from respiration, movement, waste/uneaten).
If a learner treats the shape as a separate fact, ask them to connect it to the shrinking energy at each level.
activities.rationale: A static annotated pyramid teaches the rule and shape crisply and serves well as a pre-teach or reference. Its limit, compared with an interactive leak model, is that the learner cannot test 'what if efficiency were higher?' or discover the 'no energy left' limit themselves — state this in debrief.
sourceClaims: Roughly 10% of energy is passed to the next trophic level; the rest is lost as heat from respiration, in movement, and in waste/undigested and uneaten material — this explains the pyramid shape and short chains.
learnerActions: Tap or lift each level of a labelled energy pyramid to reveal its loss breakdown: '~90% lost as heat (respiration), movement, waste; ~10% passed on'.
Read off the fixed worked example 10,000 → 1,000 → 100 → 10 kJ and restate where each lost portion goes.
Name the shape (wide base, narrow top) and explain in one sentence how it follows from the 10% rule.
activities.intendedInsight: The ~10% rule and the named loss pathways crisply introduce or revise the concept and connect the pyramid shape to the rule.

activities.title: Reason it out loud: why can't the chain be longer?
feedback: If the learner says energy 'disappears' or is 'used up', insist they name where it goes before continuing.
If the learner explains few foxes by size/strength, redirect to the small share of energy reaching the top level.
If the learner inverts the pyramid, rebuild from the 10% rule level by level.
activities.rationale: A guided discussion surfaces the reasoning behind the shape and chain length and is strongest as a debrief after seeing the leak, since the quantitative drain is more convincing when watched than only discussed.
learnerActions: Answer the prompt: 'Only about 10% of the energy at one level reaches the next. When a rabbit eats grass, what happens to the other ~90% of the grass's energy — is it destroyed?'
Name at least two places the missing energy actually goes (heat from respiration, movement, undigested waste).
Explain why a field can feed many rabbits but only a few foxes, using the energy available rather than animal size or strength.
Explain why food chains almost never have more than about five links.
activities.intendedInsight: Verbalising where the energy goes and tying predator scarcity to the energy budget distinguishes genuine energy-tracking reasoning from rote recall.

activities.title: Check the quantitative reasoning
feedback: For the calculation, confirm 10,000 → 1,000 → 100 → 10: each step is a tenth of the level below it; flag any answer that drops by a fixed amount instead of a fixed proportion.
For 'why short', require an energy-availability reason, not a restatement of '10%'.
For the fox/rabbit item, accept only answers grounded in available energy, not body size.
activities.rationale: The rule and its consequences are highly checkable, including a proportional calculation and a 'why does the pyramid narrow?' explanation item. A recognition/selection check confirms recall but does not by itself elicit the independent explanation the objective requires, so pair it with the spoken/written reasoning task.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 'Interactions and interdependencies' covers food webs and interdependence, providing the basis for explaining chain length and pyramid structure via energy transfer.
learnerActions: Given a producer level of 10,000 kJ, calculate how much energy reaches the fourth trophic level by applying ~10% three times (fill-in-the-blank proportional chain: 10,000 → 1,000 → 100 → 10 kJ).
Choose and justify why food chains are short in energy terms, rather than just naming the rule.
Put the loss pathways (heat/respiration, movement, waste, uneaten) in the right place at a transfer.
Decide whether you would expect a greater mass of foxes than of rabbits in the same field, and explain in energy terms why this is very unlikely.
activities.intendedInsight: The learner can apply the ~10% rule quantitatively and explain pyramid shape and chain-length limits, transferring the reasoning to the biomass question.

constraints: Success means explaining WHY the pyramid narrows and WHY chains are short in energy terms, not merely stating the ~10% rule.
Treat ~10% as a teaching rule of thumb, not an exact constant; real transfer efficiencies vary.
'Lost' energy is transferred out of the chain (heat from respiration, movement, undigested waste, uneaten parts), never destroyed — keep conservation of energy explicit.
Distinguish one-way energy flow (lost at each step) from matter/nutrient cycling (recycled); pupils frequently conflate these.
Keep level-labelling and the number of 10% applications consistent: from the producer level, one application reaches level 2 (1,000 kJ), two reach level 3 (100 kJ), three reach level 4 (10 kJ).

A static annotated pyramid is a scaffold: it conveys the rule and shape but cannot let the learner test efficiency changes or discover the 'no energy left' limit — reserve those for an interactive or guided-reasoning activity.
Recognition/selection tasks confirm recall but do not by themselves demonstrate independent construction of the energy-based explanation; require the learner to state the reasoning.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three cited sources (NGSS MS-LS2-3 and the ~10% rule background) were marked unverified in the source row; the ~10% figure is a standard teaching approximation and should be presented as such.

The original row judged a 3D scene as adding nothing and framed the interactive leak model as uniquely enabling discovery; those are catalog fit preferences, not established comparative efficacy, and have been softened to scoped proposals with stated affordances/limits.

Arithmetic re-checked in this independent pass: 10,000 → 1,000 → 100 → 10 is each ×0.1. Applying ~10% three times from the producer level (10,000) yields 10 kJ at the FOURTH trophic level; the third level is 100 kJ after two applications. Action, feedback and the level-labelling constraint are mutually consistent on this point.

The NGSS 'develop a model' claim on the first activity supports the modeling format of that activity (itself an energy-flow model) but is more topical than the specific compounding rationale; retained on that basis, not as evidence the activity was tested.

probeDeeper: If energy isn't destroyed, name two places the missing 90% actually goes.
Why do food chains almost never have more than about five links?
A pyramid of biomass is wide at the bottom and narrow at the top — why that shape?
Could you ever have a greater mass of foxes than of rabbits in the same field? Why not?
assess.correctAnswer: The energy is NOT destroyed — it is transferred out of the food chain, mostly as heat released during respiration, plus energy used for movement and energy lost in undigested waste (droppings). Because only about 10% passes up at each level, far less energy is available higher up, so the same field can support only a few foxes but many rabbits.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The lost 90% is destroyed / used up and gone' — violates conservation of energy.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Energy is never destroyed, only transferred; name the exits — heat from respiration, movement, undigested waste — so the 90% is accounted for.
errorPatterns.distractor: The other 90% is destroyed — it gets used up and disappears.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the missing energy 'disappears' or is 'used up', naming nowhere it goes.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'There are fewer foxes because they are bigger / stronger / eat more' — explains predator scarcity by the animals, not by available energy.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Tie numbers to the energy budget: little energy reaches the top level, so it can support little living mass there, regardless of body size.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Attributes low fox numbers to their size or power rather than to the small share of energy reaching the top.

errorPatterns.pattern: Inverts the pyramid — expects top predators to be most numerous because they 'win / are in charge'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build the pyramid from the 10% rule: each level up has ~a tenth of the energy, hence far less biomass — wide base, narrow top.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Draws or describes the biomass pyramid narrow at the bottom and wide at the top.

responseLevels.gap: Says the energy is destroyed, or explains fox scarcity by size/strength; may invert the pyramid.
responseLevels.full: States energy is transferred out as heat (respiration), movement and waste — not destroyed — and uses the ~10% transfer to explain the pyramid's shape and why chains are short, transferring to the biomass question.
responseLevels.partial: Says energy is 'lost' and there is less at the top, but cannot name the exits (heat/movement/waste) or link the 10% rule to the pyramid shape and the limit on trophic levels.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'Only about 10% of the energy at one level reaches the next. When a rabbit eats grass, what happens to the other roughly 90% of the grass's energy — is it destroyed? Then use your answer to explain why a field can feed lots of rabbits but only a few foxes.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 'Destroyed' versus 'transferred elsewhere' separates a child who breaks conservation of energy from one who tracks it leaving as heat/movement/waste. The rabbit-vs-fox part separates a child who explains predator scarcity by size or strength from one who reasons from the energy available.
